title: Cognitive Gating: The BG as a Policy Over Thought
excerpt: The preceding sections described how the basal ganglia manage the exploration-exploitation tradeoff and orchestrate the long-arc transition from goal-directed to habitual motor control. Both accounts treated the "actions" gated by the BG as overt motor outputs
html:
The preceding sections described how the basal ganglia manage the exploration-exploitation tradeoff and orchestrate the long-arc transition from goal-directed to habitual motor control. Both accounts treated the "actions" gated by the BG as overt motor outputs—movements, sequences, kinematic trajectories. But the parallel-loop architecture developed throughout this chapter implies something far more general: because the basal ganglia are embedded in limbic, associative, and sensorimotor cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops, they gate not only skeletal movements but also cognitive operations—working-memory updating, attentional set-shifting, task-set selection, strategy deployment, and the retrieval or suppression of internal goals. In this extended sense, the BG implement a policy over thought: they learn, through dopaminergic reinforcement, when to allow new information into prefrontal working memory, when to protect maintained representations from distraction, which cognitive strategy to deploy in a given context, and when to switch from one interpretive frame to another. The same opponent D1/D2 plasticity that trains motor action selection trains these cognitive gating policies; the same distributional and multi-timescale error signals that evaluate motor outcomes evaluate cognitive ones; and the same territory-specific plasticity regimes that distinguish flexible goal-directed motor learning from rigid habitual execution may, in principle, distinguish flexible cognitive strategies from deeply automatized mental routines. This section makes that abstract claim concrete.

Working-memory gating: the PBWM framework and extensions. The most fully developed computational account of BG-mediated cognitive gating is the prefrontal cortex basal ganglia working memory (PBWM) model, introduced by O’Reilly and Frank and extended in subsequent work 1, 2, 3. The core insight is architectural: prefrontal cortex maintains information through recurrent excitatory connectivity–sustained firing patterns that persist after a stimulus has been removed–but this very persistence creates a dilemma. If PFC representations are easily overwritten, they cannot serve as a stable working-memory buffer; if they are too stable, they cannot be updated when new task-relevant information arrives. The PBWM model resolves this maintenance-versus-updating tradeoff by assigning the basal ganglia the role of a learned dynamic gate. PFC is organized into separable "stripes"–anatomical clusters of interconnected neurons that are functionally isolated from other stripes–and each stripe is gated by a corresponding basal ganglia channel 1. When direct-pathway ("Go") neurons in the striatal channel fire, they disinhibit the thalamocortical loop for that stripe, triggering an update of its working-memory contents with whatever cortical input is currently active (in vivo, likely those contents held in cortical regions corresponding to the prefrontal stripe). When indirect-pathway ("NoGo") neurons dominate, the gate remains closed and the existing PFC representation is maintained against distractors. The gating decision itself–whether to open or close–is learned through dopaminergic reinforcement: positive prediction errors (dopamine bursts) potentiate corticostriatal Go synapses that were active at the time of a successful gate, while negative prediction errors (dopamine dips) potentiate NoGo synapses, gradually shaping a gating policy that admits task-relevant information and excludes irrelevant input 1. A 2025 computational model extends the PBWM framework (Figure).

This gating architecture is not limited to a single operation. The PBWM model and its descendants distinguish at least three separable gating functions: input gating (whether to encode a new item into a PFC stripe), maintenance (whether to protect the current contents of a stripe from overwriting), and output gating (which of the currently maintained items should be read out to influence downstream processing or response selection) 1, 2. The combination of input and output gating decisions made on each trial constitutes the gating policy, and it is this policy–not merely the contents of working memory–that the BG learn to optimize through reinforcement. The computational consequence is that the BG do not simply store or retrieve information; they learn a control program that governs the flow of information through prefrontal circuits, determining what enters working memory, what persists there, and what influences behavior at any given moment. A computational account distinguishes several gating operations (Figure) 25. The 2025 model simulates a sequence of gating decisions (Figure).

Empirical evidence supports key predictions of this framework. Patients with Parkinson’s disease, whose striatal dopamine depletion produces an exaggerated NoGo bias, show impaired working-memory updating while simultaneously exhibiting increased resistance to distractors—a double dissociation that follows directly from the opponent Go/NoGo architecture applied to the cognitive domain 4, 5. Dopaminergic medication reverses these effects, restoring updating at the cost of increased distractibility. Human eye-blink rate, a putative peripheral marker of phasic striatal dopamine, increases on trials that require working-memory updating and on trials that require gate switching, consistent with the PBWM prediction that both operations depend on striatal dopaminergic gating signals 6. And individual differences in genetic variants affecting striatal D1 and D2 receptor function predict individual differences in Go versus NoGo learning in probabilistic reinforcement tasks, with the effects being specific to striatal genotypes rather than prefrontal dopaminergic genotypes–consistent with the model’s assignment of the gating computation to the striatum rather than to PFC itself 7, 8. A 2025 human study separates working memory and reinforcement learning (Figure) 26. The 2025 study examines dopamine synthesis and learning (Figure). The study estimates distinct contributions from working memory and reinforcement learning (Figure).

A recent and theoretically important extension of the PBWM framework concerns adaptive chunking in working memory. This work showed that a neural network model of PFC-BG interactions can learn to reuse the same prefrontal populations to store multiple items, effectively compressing several distinct stimuli into shared PFC representations 9. This chunking strategy trades precision for capacity: by gating multiple items into the same PFC stripe, the system can hold more items in working memory, but the individual item representations become less precise. Here, the decision of whether and how to chunk is itself learned through dopaminergic reinforcement in the BG gating circuits, making it a task-dependent policy choice rather than a fixed architectural constraint. The model required a dynamic range of dopaminergic signals to adjust striatal gating policies across different working-memory demands, and the authors note that this provides a new interpretation of working-memory difficulties in clinical populations such as Parkinson’s disease, ADHD, and schizophrenia: these disorders may involve not merely a deficit in storage capacity but a failure to adaptively learn the gating policies–including chunking strategies–that determine how effectively the available capacity is used 9. From the standpoint of the BG loss landscape developed in the preceding subsections, adaptive chunking is a striking example of the BG optimizing not merely which action to take (store this item or not) but how to represent the relevant information–a policy over the format of thought, not merely its content. The resulting capacity–precision tradeoff can be illustrated by comparing chunking with slot and resource models (Figure). The chunking model is tested on recall (Figure). The simulations compare recall with and without chunking (Figure). The chunking study follows simulated gating policies (Figure).

The "actions" metaphor taken literally: cognitive operations as policy variables. The PBWM model treats working-memory gating as a cognitive "action" that the BG learn to select, but this metaphor can—and arguably should—be taken literally. In the active-inference framework, overt movements and covert cognitive operations are both policies selected under the same variational optimization logic: the agent selects among candidate policies (sequences of state transitions, whether muscular or cognitive) on the basis of expected free energy, which scores both the pragmatic value (reward, goal-satisfaction) and the epistemic value (information gain, uncertainty reduction) of each policy 10, 11, 12. In this formulation, the basal ganglia’s disinhibitory gating mechanism is not merely analogous to motor action selection; it is action selection, operating over a different action space. The ventral and dorsomedial cortico-basal ganglia loops, which receive convergent input from prefrontal, cingulate, and orbitofrontal cortices, are positioned to gate prefrontal representations that determine what cognitive "policy" is currently active–whether to maintain a working-memory trace, shift attentional focus, switch task sets, retrieve a new goal from long-term memory, or deploy a particular reasoning strategy. The dopaminergic δ\delta that evaluates motor outcomes evaluates cognitive outcomes by the same logic: a positive prediction error following a successful working-memory update, a well-timed attentional shift, or a correctly deployed strategy reinforces the corticostriatal weights that produced it, just as it would reinforce the weights that produced a successful grasp.

Recent computational work makes this unification especially explicit: they model working-memory maintenance as itself a type of policy selection within an active-inference generative model, casting the decision to hold a percept in working memory as a cognitive action implemented through PFC-basal ganglia loops 12. The formal parallel with motor gating is precise: in both cases, the BG evaluate candidate policies (gate open versus gate closed; maintain versus update; attend versus ignore) on the basis of expected free energy, and in both cases, the selected policy is executed through disinhibition of thalamocortical circuits. The implication is that the BG’s policy-optimization mandate, as described in the loss-function section, extends without modification to the cognitive domain: the same territory-specific objective functions, the same distributional and multi-timescale error signals, and the same opponent D1/D2 plasticity that optimize motor policies optimize cognitive ones, with the crucial difference being the identity of the cortical state representations over which the optimization operates. A 2026 study jointly models working memory and reinforcement learning (Figure) 27.

Frank and Badre provided one of the most detailed accounts of how this cognitive gating architecture supports hierarchical cognitive control. In their model, nested cortico-striatal circuits at different rostro-caudal levels of frontal cortex each gate cognitive representations at a particular level of abstraction 13. More anterior (rostral) frontal regions maintain more abstract contextual representations—task rules, category-level goals—and their BG gating circuits learn to selectively admit higher-order contextual information. More posterior (caudal) frontal regions maintain more concrete stimulus-response mappings, and their gating is modulated by the output of the rostral circuits. The result is a hierarchy of learned gating policies in which the BG at each level learn, through dopaminergic reinforcement, which contextual information should be gated into PFC at that level of abstraction. Functional MRI evidence confirmed key predictions: rostral prefrontal and striatal activations tracked the discovery of abstract hierarchical rules in a reinforcement-learning task, and the computational model’s trial-by-trial estimates of latent hypothesis states predicted the BOLD signal in individual cortico-striatal circuits at specific levels of policy abstraction 14. This finding extends the BG’s domain from simple action selection to the kind of structured, multi-level cognitive control that supports human reasoning, planning, and rule use.

Reinforcement learning over strategies: meta-learning and the prefrontal-BG system. The hierarchical gating architecture just described allows the BG to learn which task rules and contextual representations to maintain; but the most powerful form of cognitive gating may be the BG’s role in learning strategies themselves. Collins and Frank showed that human learning on multi-stimulus, multi-response tasks is not well described by a single reinforcement-learning system but instead reflects the interaction of at least two partially dissociable systems: an incremental BG-dependent RL system and a prefrontal working-memory system that can maintain recent stimulus-response mappings in a fast, capacity-limited buffer 15. The relative contribution of these two systems depends on task demands—set size, delay, interference—and the BG learn not only the stimulus-response mappings themselves but also the task-set structure: which stimuli should be grouped under the same abstract rule, which rules should be created anew versus retrieved from a library of previously learned task sets, and how policies should be transferred and composed across novel situations 16, 17. In these models, the BG gating circuitry operates at two levels simultaneously: at the lower level, it gates specific stimulus-response mappings; at the higher level, it gates the selection of the abstract task set under which those mappings are organized. Dopaminergic reinforcement operates at both levels, enabling the system to perform conditional "if-then" hypothesis testing and to discover hierarchical structure through experience 13. The 2026 study compares model predictions with behavior (Figure). The 2026 study examines neural correlates of learning systems (Figure). The 2026 analysis relates model estimates to neural decision dynamics (Figure).

Wang, Kurth-Nelson, Kumaran, and colleagues pushed this logic further, proposing that the dopaminergic system trains prefrontal cortex not merely to implement a fixed policy but to operate as its own free-standing meta-learning system 18. In their account, slow dopamine-dependent corticostriatal plasticity shapes the recurrent dynamics of PFC over many tasks, such that PFC acquires a general-purpose learning algorithm implemented in its own activation dynamics. This "meta-learned" PFC system can then adapt rapidly to new tasks—within a single episode—without requiring further synaptic change, because the adaptation occurs through the fast dynamics of prefrontal activity rather than through slow weight modification. The BG’s role in this framework is to provide the slow outer-loop optimization that sculpts prefrontal dynamics over the developmental and experiential timescale: dopaminergic prediction errors, broadcasting through corticostriatal loops, gradually tune the recurrent connectivity of PFC until its fast dynamics implement an efficient learning algorithm for the kinds of tasks the organism regularly encounters. This is RL over RL: the BG learn a policy for how to learn, not merely a policy for what to do.

The meta-learning framework has a natural interpretation in terms of the territory-specific loss landscape developed earlier. The ventral and dorsomedial striatal loops, which operate on longer temporal horizons and receive convergent input from prefrontal, cingulate, and orbitofrontal cortices, are well positioned to learn the abstract, slowly changing strategic variables—which task set to deploy, which learning rate to use, which information to attend to—that constitute the meta-policy. The dorsolateral loops, operating on shorter horizons, may then implement the concrete motor and cognitive actions dictated by the currently active strategy. In this picture, strategy selection and meta-learning are simply the highest levels of a hierarchical policy that the BG optimize across their full territory-specific gradient, from abstract goals (ventromedial) through intermediate action-outcome contingencies (dorsomedial) to concrete motor execution (dorsolateral). The same dopaminergic teaching signals, parameterized by different discount factors, asymmetric error scalings, and cholinergic gating regimes, operate at each level—but the "actions" they evaluate become progressively more abstract as one ascends the hierarchy.

This perspective connects to a broader set of cognitive competences that can be reframed as BG-gated policies over internal operations. Metamemory—the monitoring of one’s own memory confidence and the strategic allocation of encoding effort—can be understood as a gating policy over hippocampal-prefrontal memory encoding: the BG learn when it is worth investing cognitive resources in committing an experience to memory and when those resources are better deployed elsewhere. Metacognition more broadly—the evaluation of one’s own decision-making process, including judgments of confidence, the decision to seek more information, and the decision to commit to a choice—partially maps onto the STN-mediated threshold-adjustment and conflict-monitoring computations described in the loss-function section, but applied to the cognitive rather than the motor domain: the BG regulate how much evidence to accumulate before committing to a cognitive judgment, just as they regulate how much evidence to accumulate before committing to a motor action 19. Game strategy and social reasoning—choosing which interpersonal or competitive strategy to deploy in a multi-agent setting—likewise require the selection of abstract, context-dependent cognitive policies; the BG’s associative loops, receiving input from prefrontal and cingulate cortices that represent social and strategic variables, are positioned to gate these selections through the same disinhibitory mechanism that gates motor actions. In each of these domains, the formal structure is the same: cortex represents the space of possible cognitive operations, and the BG evaluate, select, and reinforce particular operations on the basis of dopaminergic credit assignment.

Speculative extension: cognitive habitization and the rigidity of mental routines. The skill-acquisition section described in detail how the BG orchestrate a progressive transfer of behavioral control from flexible, goal-directed, DMS-dependent policies to rigid, automatized, DLS-dependent habits. The question naturally arises: does a parallel transfer occur for cognitive routines? If the BG gate cognitive operations through the same cortico-basal ganglia loops that gate motor actions, and if these loops are subject to the same territory-specific plasticity regimes that differentiate DMS from DLS, then it is at least plausible that well-practiced cognitive strategies—habitual modes of attention, reflexive interpretive frames, automatic emotional appraisals, default reasoning heuristics—undergo a similar transition from flexible, outcome-sensitive, "goal-directed" cognitive control to rigid, stimulus-bound, "habitual" cognitive control.

Several lines of evidence, though none definitive, support this speculation. First, at the behavioral level, cognitive routines clearly become more automatic with practice: expert chess players, experienced clinicians, and fluent readers all deploy complex cognitive operations that were once effortful and deliberate in a rapid, seemingly reflexive manner, with reduced demands on attentional resources and reduced sensitivity to the details of the current context—precisely the behavioral signatures of the goal-directed-to-habitual transition in the motor domain. Second, neuroimaging studies of skill learning across cognitive and motor domains report a common pattern in which prefrontal and parietal attentional-control regions show decreasing activation with practice, while striatal and premotor regions show increasing or reorganized activation—a pattern that is at least consistent with a shift from dorsomedial (associative) to dorsolateral (sensorimotor) cortico-basal ganglia engagement, though the imaging evidence cannot by itself confirm a DMS-to-DLS transfer for cognitive routines 20, 21. Third, Graybiel’s influential definition of habits emphasizes that they extend beyond motor behaviors to include cognitive processes, and recent work on "attentional habits" shows that learned attentional biases can exhibit hallmark properties of motor habits—automaticity, insensitivity to outcome devaluation, and inflexibility—suggesting that at least some forms of attention are governed by the same corticostriatal habit machinery that governs motor routines 22.

The critical question, however, is whether the DMS-to-DLS transfer mechanism documented for motor habits operates in the cognitive domain. Here the evidence is more ambiguous. The executive loop connecting lateral prefrontal cortex with the caudate (the primate homolog of DMS) does not have a cleanly established "habitual" counterpart in the sensorimotor putamen (DLS homolog) for purely cognitive routines; the cognitive and motor loops, while sharing architectural principles, involve partially distinct cortical territories and may not be organized in exactly the same hierarchical gradient 21. Baladron and Hamker’s hierarchical model of multiple BG loops offers one possible resolution: in their framework, each loop learns to select intermediate objectives at a different abstraction level, and a learned "shortcut" pathway that bypasses the higher loops can link stimulus information directly with motor execution, providing the motor loops with less cognitive influence and leading to faster, more habitual behavior 23. Applied to the cognitive domain, an analogous shortcut might allow well-practiced cognitive operations—initially mediated by the associative (DMS) loop in a flexible, context-sensitive manner—to be triggered more directly by stimuli through cortico-cortical connections that have been trained by BG-dependent learning but no longer require BG gating for execution. This is precisely the mechanism by which Helie, Ashby, and colleagues proposed that the BG train robust cortico-cortical connections during initial learning, which then support automatized performance independently of BG involvement 20.

If cognitive habitization does occur through mechanisms analogous to motor habitization, the implications would be far-reaching. Well-practiced attentional biases—the tendency to interpret ambiguous stimuli in a particular way, to deploy a particular reasoning heuristic by default, or to appraise emotional situations through a particular evaluative frame—might shift from flexible, outcome-sensitive, DMS-mediated control to rigid, stimulus-bound, automatized routines that are resistant to extinction and insensitive to devaluation, just as motor habits are. The asymmetric anti-Hebbian STDP regime in DLS, the positively biased dopamine signals, and the progressive structural consolidation of corticostriatal ensembles described in the plasticity section would all favor the durability and inflexibility of these cognitive habits. This could help explain why some cognitive styles—chronic worry patterns, ruminative thinking, rigid interpretive frames in psychopathology, but also adaptive expertise and fluent professional judgment—are so resistant to deliberate revision: they may have been compiled into corticostriatal weight configurations whose plasticity regime actively resists rewriting, just as overtrained motor habits resist extinction even after reward contingencies have changed 24. The therapeutic difficulty of dislodging deeply practiced maladaptive cognitive habits—a central challenge in cognitive-behavioral therapy and related interventions—may thus reflect not merely a motivational or insight deficit, but a genuine circuit-level rigidity inherited from the same DLS plasticity machinery that makes motor habits durable.

This account should be flagged as speculative. The evidence for a complete DMS-to-DLS transfer in purely cognitive routines remains indirect, and the cognitive and motor cortico-basal ganglia loops may differ in ways that preclude a simple isomorphism. Moreover, the degree to which "cognitive habits" are truly BG-dependent—as opposed to being stored in cortico-cortical connections that were initially trained by BG mechanisms but subsequently operate autonomously—remains an open question. What can be said with reasonable confidence is that the BG’s policy-optimization machinery is not confined to the motor domain; that the same opponent D1/D2 plasticity, dopaminergic credit assignment, and hierarchical gating architecture that select and reinforce motor actions also select and reinforce cognitive operations including working-memory updating, task-set selection, strategy deployment, and attentional allocation; and that the territory-specific and training-dependent plasticity regimes that differentiate flexible from habitual motor control provide at least a plausible neural substrate for the analogous distinction between flexible and automatized cognitive control. The BG, on this view, are not merely the brain’s motor optimizer. They are its general-purpose policy optimizer—a system that learns, through dopaminergic reinforcement, which cortical computations to gate, energize, suppress, or automatize, whether those computations produce a movement, a memory update, or a thought.
